translations.text: The life of our beloved brother Apa Paul of Tamma, who went to his rest on the seventh day of the month of Paopi. May his blessing come upon us, and may we be saved in the peace of God. Amen. Listen, you who love to listen, to the voice which is [?].
[?] Just as he said to his disciples, “If you keep my commandments [?], you will remain in them [?].”
[?] God sent Michael the archangel to me at noon on the sixteenth of Epip. He said to me, “Greetings, my honored son.” I answered him, “Greetings to you too [?].”
[?] is the man from Tamma. For you are the one who will take charge of his body when he lays his body down.
When he had said these things, he went to heaven in glory. I immediately got up and stopped under [?] [?].
[?] is equal. John said, “Let it be so, our father and our bishop.” Peter said, “My father Paul, rise and call upon God to send us bread
from heaven, so that we may eat together.” My father said, “Forgive me; bless me. Rise, and let us pray to him, and he will grant our request.” They rose and stretched out their hands
together. My father called upon God, saying, “My Lord Jesus Christ, you who blessed five loaves, and five hundred people ate and were satisfied with the five barley loaves
and the two fish; you who heard Elisha and satisfied a thousand people with the ten barley loaves, hear me today. You who heard Daniel when he was in the lions’ den
and sent Habakkuk to him with the meal in his hands, hear me today and send me bread from heaven, so that I may eat with my brothers and my fathers.” Immediately,
a table appeared, with a platter on it and three hot loaves on the platter, and they came to rest in our midst. My father said to them, “Rise, and let us eat some of the bread from heaven.”
He also took a little salt and put it on the table. We prayed together and ate the little bread with the Lord’s blessing. My father spoke and said to the brothers, “I tell you
that it has been fifty-four years, from the day when my beloved father Apa Hyperechius cut my hair on the mountain until now. A single loaf is allotted to me by God every forty

days, along with a measure of water. I do not know where they come from. I eat some of them on the evening of my fortieth day, and I do not eat again until the completion of my next forty days, according to the commandment the Savior gave us
in the holy Gospel. He himself neither ate nor drank for forty days and forty nights.” The brothers said to him, “You do well. No warrior receives a crown unless he fights well.” He raised
his hands toward heaven and prayed with the brothers, saying, “Lord Jesus Christ, King of kings, hear us today and send us bread that is hot and fresh.” Immediately, there were [?]

from heaven, and they came to rest in our midst, wrapped in linen cloths. Peter said to John, “Here are the bread and the cloths. We also need the preparations for the offering.” John answered and said to the brothers, “Pray for me, so that I may do what he [?].”
[?] John opened his mouth and said, “Our Lord Jesus Christ, send a table from heaven, so that we may place your body on it
and your blood.” Immediately, a golden table came from heaven and came to rest in our midst. Paul also rose and prayed in this way, saying, “My Lord
Jesus Christ, you who called me to a place among the holy apostles, although I was formerly a persecutor, persecuting his holy bride, the Church,
now, Lord, hear me in the midst of my brothers and send me from heaven a cup filled with wine from the true vine.” At that very moment, a cup filled
with wine from the true vine came to rest on the table. The elder Apa Isidore, the priest, also rose, lifted both his hands toward heaven, and prayed, saying:
“Lord God Almighty, King of kings, I am not worthy to speak among my brothers and your chosen ones, whom you chose for yourself as apostles. But because of the joy you have given me,
I rose and called upon you, asking you to grant my request and send me incense from the incense of paradise, so that we might set it down until we invoke your name over your body
and your holy blood.” Immediately, a bowl full of incense appeared in the midst of us, and we were immersed in the incense. Apa Agathonicus, from the mountain of [?], also rose. “Take,” he said, [?].
[?] crumbs that remained of [?] were being put into my father’s basket. I drank the water in the measure. We prayed and left that place. We went south through the whole mountain. [?]

[?] the brother monks [?]. We heard a voice saying, “[?] bless us, Apa Paul of Tamma and Ezekiel of Little Terot. Come in, saints of the Lord! Welcome to us, Apa Paul of Tamma, whom the Lord raised [?].
[?] you here today.” My father said, “Welcome, Apa Pamun, you with the robe of many colors [?], like that of Joseph, the righteous king.
He asked him again, “Who shaved your head?” He said, “It was my father Apa Hellen. Remember me, my holy father, Apa [?].”
“My father, [?] where do you gather for worship on Saturday and Sunday?” Apa Pamun answered, “John the Virgin is the one who holds the worship service on Saturday and Sunday. For on Saturday [?].”
As for Apa Apollo, we found him sitting on a throne, teaching his children the commandments of life. When he saw my father Apa Paul, he sprang up from his throne
and approached him, kissed him, and said, “Welcome to us today, Christ’s prize of victory, Apa Paul, whom the Lord raised from the dead five
times. He will raise you again, just as he told you. And the seventh time he raises you will be on the day of the resurrection of all the saints.”
After Apa Apollo said this, he had all the people gathered together. He went to the church, and we gathered for worship with the holy offering. He sent the brothers to the dining room, but he took us
to the service quarters and had food prepared for us to eat. My father, however, did not want to eat, because he had spent three days fasting during Lent. But our father Apa Apollo stood up

and urged him, saying, “Please listen to me, my father, and eat with me, so that a blessing may come upon my dwelling and my monastery today because of you. You know, my beloved father, that what goes into the mouth
of a person is not what defiles that person. So now, my father, listen to me and eat with me.” My father agreed to eat with Apa Apollo. I too, along with my companion, ate together
with the rest of the brothers who were with us. These were their names: Apa Paese, Apa Nishkroou, Apa Soures, and Apa Pita. When we had finished eating, at evening our father Apa
Apollo came among us and clapped his hands together, saying, “Let whoever has received wings fly away.” At that very moment Apa Paese flew away and hurried to the mountain of Hace.
Apa Nishkroou also flew away and went to the mountain north of Antinoë. Apa Pitta also flew away and went to the mountain of Asyut. When [?] came, our father Apa Apollo accompanied us out

to the south of the monastery as well. He embraced us and sent us away in peace. We traveled south through Mount Tereb until we reached Mount Terotashans, south of Qus. We found some antelopes down below,
grazing, with a monk among them. My father went forward and greeted him. He said to him, “What is your name?” He said, “My name is Aphou. Remember me, my father Apa Paul,

so that the Lord may bring me to a good end.” My father said to him, “How many years have you been here?” He said, “Fifty-four years.” My father asked him again, “Who clothed you in the monastic habit?” He said, “Apa

Anthony of Scetis.” My father said to him, “Then what do you live on as you travel with these antelopes?” He said, “My food and that of these antelopes are the same: the plants of the field and these [?].”

My father said to him, “Do you not get cold in winter or suffer from the heat in summer?” He said to him, “When it is winter, I sleep among these gazelles, and they warm me with the breath from their mouths. When
it is summer, they gather together, stand up, and shade me so that the scorching heat does not trouble me.” My father said to him, “Truly, you deserve to be called Apa Aphou the Gazelle.”
At that moment a voice came to us, saying, “This is his name throughout all the generations of the earth.”
We were amazed at what had happened so quickly. We greeted him, left him, and walked south to the mountain of Pshchepohe. We found a dwelling to our west.
My father knocked on the stone three times, according to the rule of the monastic brothers.
Immediately we heard a faint voice saying, “Bless me, my holy fathers.”
Then he came out and opened the door for us. We bowed down before him and greeted him.
His body had become extremely thin from hunger and thirst. He took us into the dwelling. We prayed, sat down, and spoke about the mighty deeds of God.
My father said to him, “What is your name?”
He answered, saying, “My name is Phib, and I am from Perchous in the district of Touho.”
My father said to him, “How many years has it been since you came to this place?”
He said, “It has been eighteen years [?].”
My father said to him, “How long will you remain in this place?”
He said to him again, “This is my dwelling in life and in death.”
My father said to him, “What do you eat, or what do you drink, or who attends to your needs?”
The holy Apa Phib answered, “From the time of my childhood, when I left my home, until today,
wherever I live, each time I complete my forty-day fast, I find a loaf of bread and a jug of water set before me.
“And God is my witness that, since that time, only one loaf has been allotted to me each time.”
But when you came to me today with your disciple, look, God sent us food for the three of us.
Now get up, and let us taste a little bread, as God has commanded.”

We got up, stretched out our hands, and prayed. We stretched ourselves out and ate together from a single loaf. We also drank a little water. We left our father Apa Phoeb, and he sent us on our way in peace.
We traveled south through the whole mountain region until we came to Mount Meroit, and we found ourselves a place to live there.
I was sitting alone in the dwelling when a man came to the door and called to me.
I went outside to see what was happening.
He said to me, “Are you Ezekiel?”
I said to him, “Yes, I am.”
He said to me, “Let me inside the door of your dwelling so that I can tell you this matter.
I do not want to say it where the brothers might hear and become frightened.”
Because of his pleasant way of speaking, I took him inside.
He said to me, “My brother Ezekiel, do you know what has happened?”
I said, “No.”

He said to me, “Yesterday at the seventh hour, I was walking in the desert with some other men, looking for stones to make into lime [?]. We encountered robbers in the mountains, and they took our tools from us. We barely managed to escape from them alive.
When we escaped from their hands, we came upon a large man, tied up and lying in a valley.
We untied him.”
He said to us, “Leave me here. But when you go to the mountain, you will find this dwelling place. Call inside, ‘Ezekiel!’”
Your father said, “Come to me in the desert, for the robbers rose up and bound me, wanting to kill me. But God rescued my soul from their hands.”
We asked him, “What is your name?”
He said to us, “My name is Paul, and I am from Tamma in the district of Kois.”
When I, Ezekiel, heard these things, I was shaken because he had spoken my father’s name and the name of his village.
That man said to me again, “Get up and follow me, and I will take you to him, for I see that you are afraid.”
I walked with him throughout the desert. I spent the first day and the second day walking.
I said to him, “Have we not yet reached that place?”
He said, “No. We had reached the third [?] day of walking in the desert.”
I said to him again, “Have we still not reached him?”
He said, “Look, we have come close to him.”
While he was speaking with me, he changed and became a huge Ethiopian. His eyes were full of blood, his whole body was covered with hair, and he stank like billy goats.
He said to me, “Did you not recognize me, Ezekiel?”
I said to him, “No.” He said to me, “I was the one making the spring run dry at that time. Your father struck me until I filled it again as it had been before.
I suffered when I rose against you and your father, but you did not become wise.”
I said to him, “So you are the devil! May the Lord rebuke you for all the evil things you have done to Christ’s servants.”
He lunged after me like a wild lion, wanting to kill me.
But I cried out, “My father, help me!”
Immediately my father heard my voice as though he were close to me. He got up at once and came to me through God’s help.

When my father approached him, the devil immediately changed and took the appearance of a monk, wearing a skin and small palm-leaf garments. He bowed to my father and fell at his feet according to the custom of the monastic brothers.
Immediately my father struck him around the side of his monastic robe, [?], because he recognized that he was the devil.
He seized him, bound him hand and foot, and rolled him down into a ditch. We left him and went away.
I said to my father, “What is this thing you have done to this shameless creature?”
My father said to me, “God has handed him over to me so that I may punish him as I wish, because he dared to tempt us.”
After my father said these things, we got up and returned to our dwelling, giving glory to God.

My father spent forty days and forty nights without eating or drinking, sitting on a brick inside the dwelling and staring at a window through an opening. He did not close his eyes during these forty days, until they burst and fell out onto the ground.
The holy archangel came from heaven—that is, Michael the archangel—at dawn on Sunday, at the completion of the forty days.
He placed a seal on him and relieved him of all his sufferings. His eyes were restored immediately, and Michael the archangel went up to heaven in glory.
We gathered with the brothers who were with us in that place and ate with them on Sunday. Then we left them in peace.
We went south to the rock of Asyut and obtained a small dwelling for ourselves there.
My father practiced great acts of ascetic discipline.
One day a great saint of God came to us. His name was Apa Bishoy of Jeremiah, and he lived in the mountain of Qaw, east of the river.
We greeted one another, prayed, and sat down. We spoke about the mighty deeds of Christ and the ways of life of the saints.
When they had finished arguing with one another, we got up and walked in the mountain. We found a rock full of bones. They were all idol worshipers.
When the saints reached them, they stood and prayed over them. They all rose alive, numbering six hundred men and fifty-four women.
The saints said to them, “What is your occupation?”
One of them answered, saying, “Listen to me, holy ones, and I will tell you about our wickedness and our lawlessness.
For we are a single nation, worshiping a wild animal called the wolf. We care for it at all times, offering it little children three years old as sacrifices.
It encouraged us, saying, ‘Do things like this for me,’ and other deeds worse than these, which we do not wish to speak of.
Now, therefore, my holy fathers, let your mercy reach us and baptize us as Christians, for the distress upon us is great.”
Christ’s bridegroom, Apa Bishoy of Jeremiah, answered, “Get up, and let us pray to God so that he may give us assurance concerning this matter.”
My father said, “Let us pray.”
They rose and called upon God together, saying, “God, the merciful and compassionate one, who sent his only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ our Lord, who died for the creature he had formed,

having set the world free through the blessing of holy baptism, have compassion on these servants of yours who stand here today, awaiting your mercy and your compassion, so that they may receive forgiveness [?]
